title: Umbria's Methane Is Sprinting: Up 18.7% in Eight Weeks While Petrol and Diesel Climb in Lockstep With Italy
dek: On 17 September, self-service petrol, diesel and methane in Umbria all sit below the national average, but the weekly data shows all three rising fast and methane rising fastest.
executive_summary: Where things stand today: the latest Umbria figures, dated 17 September 2026, put self-service Benzina at €2.1427/l, Gasolio at €2.2598/l and Metano at €1.7177/kg. Each is cheaper than the national self-service average (€2.1539, €2.2924 and €1.7718), by 1.12 cents on petrol, 3.26 cents on diesel and 5.41 cents on methane. LPG is the exception: with no self-service LPG price reported in the region, the served price of €0.7728/l is 1.64 cents above the national served average of €0.7564/l. All three fuels with a self-service price rose on the day, and methane rose most.

Zoom out to the weekly averages and the story is a broad and steep climb. Between the week starting 20 July (W30) and the week starting 14 September (W38), Umbria's self-service Benzina rose 7.87%, Gasolio 4.08% and Metano 18.73%, against 8.15%, 4.24% and 16.92% for Italy as a whole. Petrol and diesel are tracking the national curve almost step for step. Methane is the fuel breaking away: in the latest week it rose 4.36% on the week before, while the national methane average rose 3.07%. The gap to the national price is closing, from 8.64 cents in W30 to 7.54 cents in W38.

fuel_sections.heading: Petrol: another cent and a bit higher, still half a percent under the national price
paragraphs: Self-service Benzina in Umbria averaged €2.1427/l on 17 September, up 1.07 cents (0.50%) from €2.1320/l the day before. The national self-service average was €2.1539/l, so Umbria sits 1.12 cents, or 0.52%, below it. At the pump with an attendant the picture is the same: €2.2806/l served in Umbria against €2.2911/l nationally, a gap of 1.05 cents. The self-service discount is worth about 13.8 cents per litre against the served price.

The weekly series shows a steady and then accelerating ramp. Regional self-service Benzina went from €1.9696/l in W30 to €2.1247/l in W38, a rise of 7.87% against 8.15% nationally. The middle of the window was quiet: W32 at €2.0028/l and W33 at €1.9992/l were essentially flat, and from W33 to W38 the price climbed 6.28% (nationally 6.81%). The last two weekly steps are the sharpest: W37 came in at €2.0784/l and W38 at €2.1247/l, each about 2.2% higher than the week before. Note that W38 covers only four days of data, and W36 only three, so the most recent weekly figures are partial-week averages.

fuel_sections.heading: Diesel: 3.3 cents cheaper than Italy, and the premium over petrol is shrinking
paragraphs: Umbrian self-service Gasolio closed at €2.2598/l on 17 September, up 1.56 cents (0.70%) from €2.2442/l on the 16th. That is 3.26 cents, or 1.42%, below the national self-service average of €2.2924/l and the second-widest discount to Italy among the self-service fuels after methane. On the served side the regional price is €2.4027/l against €2.4408/l nationally. Diesel is now 11.71 cents above petrol in Umbria on a self-service basis, versus 13.85 cents nationally.

Diesel had the most eventful path of the three fuels. It started the window at €2.1493/l (W30), fell to a trough of €2.0933/l in both W32 and W33, then climbed to €2.2370/l in W38. Over the whole window that is a net rise of 4.08%, well below petrol's 7.87%, because diesel began high. From the W33 trough the rise is 6.86%, compared with 7.27% nationally. The daily history explains the early dip: on 28 July regional diesel was €2.1687/l and on 29 July it dropped to €2.0686/l, a one-day fall of 10 cents. The diesel premium over petrol has narrowed from 15.88 cents on 21 July to 11.71 cents today, a sign that petrol has been catching up.

fuel_sections.heading: LPG: no self-service price in Umbria, and a quiet, slightly dearer served market
paragraphs: Umbria reports no self-service GPL price at all in the data, so the regional picture rests on the served price: €0.7728/l on 17 September, down 0.0003 from €0.7731/l the day before. Nationally, self-service GPL averaged €0.7558/l and served GPL €0.7564/l. The comparison that matters, served against served, puts Umbria at 1.64 cents (2.17%) above the national figure, making LPG the only tracked fuel where the region is dearer than Italy.

LPG is also the one fuel that is not rising. Across the 51 days of Umbrian history since 21 July, the served price moved only within a band of €0.7716/l to €0.7772/l, a spread of about half a cent. Nationally, weekly self-service GPL slipped from €0.7592/l in W30 to €0.7550/l in W38, a fall of 0.55%. The regional weekly self-service series is empty for lack of reported prices, so no regional weekly percentage change can be given. The contrast with methane, which has climbed 18.73% in the same weeks, is the sharpest in the data: two gas-based fuels, moving in opposite directions.

fuel_sections.heading: Methane: the fastest climber, up 18.7% in eight weeks and 3 cents in a day
paragraphs: Self-service Metano in Umbria averaged €1.7177/kg on 17 September, up 3.11 cents (1.84%) from €1.6866/kg the day before, the biggest one-day move of any fuel in the region. It is still the fuel with the widest discount to the national self-service average of €1.7718/kg: 5.41 cents, or 3.05%. The served price of €1.8204/kg is close to the national served average of €1.8344/kg, a gap of just 1.40 cents, so nearly all of the regional advantage is on the self-service side.

The weekly trend is the headline of this report. Umbria's self-service methane went from €1.4135/kg in W30 to €1.6783/kg in W38, a rise of 18.73% against 16.92% nationally. Between W33 and W38 the regional rise was 11.83%, essentially the same as the 11.68% national figure, so the outperformance was built earlier, in the first weeks of the window. It is now accelerating again: W37 to W38 is +4.36% in Umbria against +3.07% for Italy. Methane in the region moves in steps rather than a smooth line: it was flat at €1.6221/kg from 10 to 14 September and then jumped to €1.6866/kg on the 15th, a rise of 6.45 cents in a single day. Since 21 July the self-service price is up 23.27%, from €1.3934/kg.

network_section.heading: The network: 481 registered stations, 91% reporting
paragraphs: The regional registry lists 481 active stations in Umbria, about 2.0% of the 24,003 in the national registry. On 17 September, 438 of them reported prices, a reporting rate of 91.06%. Nationally the figure was 21,672 of 24,003, or 90.29%, so Umbria reports slightly better than the country as a whole. The remaining 43 stations either did not submit prices that day or are registered but effectively dormant.

The regional network is remarkably stable. Across the 51 days of Umbrian history since 21 July, the registered count never moved from 481 and the reporting count stayed between 435 and 439. A reporting rate that steady matters for the trend analysis above: the weekly averages are not being pushed around by stations dropping in and out of the sample, so the price movements reflect real price changes rather than changes in who is reporting. With around 43 non-reporting stations, though, the averages remain estimates of the regional market rather than a complete census of it.

methodology_section.heading: How this report was made: no spreadsheet, no human in the loop
paragraphs: Everything in this report was produced automatically, today, by an unattended pipeline built with Claude Code. A scheduled job pulls the latest official price and registry data from MIMIT, rebuilds the dashboard's data files, and rotates through Italy's 20 regions alphabetically by calendar date, which is why Umbria is today's spotlight and no editor picked it. The same job then computes the weekly regional and national averages for each fuel, and Claude reads the resulting numbers and writes the analysis you are reading, including every percentage cited here, checked against the data file rather than estimated.

Contrast that with the way this would normally be done: an analyst downloads a CSV, pastes it into a spreadsheet, rebuilds the pivot tables, updates the charts, writes the commentary and formats a document, every day, for every region. It takes an hour or more, it goes stale the moment someone skips a day, and it does not scale to twenty regions and four fuels. The pipeline does it unattended in minutes, publishes the interactive dashboard to the web, and leaves a person only the review and approval step before anything is shared. The data and the analysis are always in sync because they come from the same run.

pull_quote: Umbria's self-service methane has climbed 18.7% in eight weeks, outrunning Italy's 16.9%, while LPG stood still.
caption:
Today's Fuel Dashboard spotlight region is Umbria, and the most interesting number is methane: self-service Metano is up 18.7% since the week of 20 July (€1.4135 to €1.6783/kg), ahead of Italy's 16.9%, and it gained another 4.4% week on week against 3.1% nationally. Petrol (+7.9%) and diesel (+4.1%) are rising broadly in step with the national curve, while LPG has barely moved.

Fuel Dashboard is an interactive, self-updating view of Italian fuel prices by region, province, municipality, operator and brand, built on the official MIMIT open data. Every day it refreshes itself, picks a region to spotlight, and writes a full report with trend analysis for petrol, diesel, LPG and methane. Take a look: https://adeo-blip.github.io/fuel-price-italy/

The point is not just the fuel prices. This whole pipeline, from data download to analysis to the published dashboard and this report, was built with Claude Code and runs unattended. The same job in a manual Excel workbook would mean re-downloading, re-pasting, rebuilding charts and rewriting commentary every single day, and it would go stale the first day someone skipped it. AI tools let one person build something that maintains itself.
